opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the number of people truly iterating on any one generation of the model is much smaller than the headcount suggests. On a team of around a hundred, the core group pushing a given generation forward, the people making daily decisions on data, training recipes, and evaluation, might be a couple dozen at most. Sometimes it's even fewer.

That's not because everyone else isn't contributing. It's how the work is structured. Part of the team is building infrastructure: training frameworks, cluster stability, inference efficiency. That work enables every generation but isn't tied to one. Another group is doing exploratory research on ideas that might not land until the next generation or the one after. Others work on data pipelines, evaluation systems, and post-training, which feed into the main line but run on their own rhythm.

When I think about whether we're set up well, I don't count heads. I ask a few questions. Is the core iteration loop tight enough that a small group can make a decision and see the result quickly? Are the exploratory people close enough to the main line that good ideas actually get absorbed rather than sitting in a side branch? And is anyone stuck doing work that nobody downstream is waiting for?

In my experience, a model generation is driven by a fairly small, very high-density group. Adding more people to that core often slows it down, because communication cost grows faster than output. So the real skill is keeping the center small and sharp while making sure the larger team around it is building the things the next iteration will need.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, if you look at the whole hundred-person team, the number of people who are really in the loop on a single model generation—touching the core recipe, making decisions about data, architecture, training dynamics—is much smaller than people assume. I'd say it's on the order of ten to twenty people. Everyone else is doing work that's absolutely necessary but sits one or two layers out: infrastructure, data pipelines, evaluation tooling, inference, product integration.

And I think that's healthy, actually. Pretraining a frontier model is not a problem you can parallelize across a hundred brains. There's a very tight core of decisions, and if too many people are pulling on it, you lose coherence. The model ends up reflecting committee compromises rather than a clear thesis about what matters.

So the way I think about it is less "how many people are iterating" and more "how fast can the small core iterate, and how well does the rest of the team remove friction for them." If the ten people in the middle can run an experiment and get a clean signal back in a day instead of a week, that's worth more than adding thirty more researchers to the core.

The hard part is making sure the people outside the core still feel ownership. That's a management problem more than a technical one. You want someone running the data pipeline to understand why a particular filtering decision changes the model's behavior downstream, not just execute a ticket. When that works, the effective number of people contributing to the model is higher than the headcount in the room making the final call.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention interns or say their work may not appear in the current model generation.

r002.rationale: It estimates that about ten to twenty people iterate on a generation, not the criterion’s typical twenty to thirty.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish the size of the team from the number of people directly iterating on a particular model generation. A hundred-person team doesn’t mean a hundred people are all changing the same model. Some people work on data, some on infrastructure, and some on evaluation. Those contributions are essential, but the group directly driving a given iteration is smaller. So I’d assess it by looking at who is actively proposing experiments, running them, interpreting the results, and deciding what to change next, rather than by counting the whole team.
